title: My GitHub Repository Got More Clones. But Does That Mean More Users?
summary:
I've been working on a small project called NomadOS.

It's a digital product automation system built around four tools:

  • Payhip
  • Make
  • Telegram
  • Notion

Recently, I checked my GitHub traffic statistics and noticed something interesting.

My repository showed:

  • 39 clones in the last 14 days
  • 33 unique cloners
  • 15 total views
  • Only 2 unique visitors

At first, the increase in clones looked encouraging.

But then I started thinking:

Does a repository clone actually mean someone is using your project?

Not necessarily.

A clone doesn't tell you whether someone has successfully installed the project, tested the workflow, or used it in a real business.

And page views alone don't tell the whole story either.

I'm starting to look at project growth differently.

title: Fender serial number lookup in JavaScript: why E412345 can mean the USA or Japan

  • USA, 1984 to 1988. "E4 + 5 digits" is a row on the American chart.
  • Japan, 1984 to 1987. "E + 6 digits" is a row on the Japanese chart.

Both patterns match the same seven characters. The serial alone can't decide. What decides is printed right next to it: the decal that says Made in USA or Made in Japan.

I built a Fender serial number lookup for Who Actually Makes. Every rule in it comes from Fender's support articles, and the build checks every rule against a saved copy of those articles. That question took on more urgency as we worked with teams running self-hosted Pulumi Cloud in air-gapped networks or inside FedRAMP authorization boundaries.
